content.title: About
content.content: Thousand Island dressing is a classic American condiment made from a base of mayonnaise, ketchup, and finely chopped pickled vegetables. It has a sweet‑tangy flavor with a hint of spice and is commonly used on salads, sandwiches, and burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Thousand Islands region between the United States and Canada, where the sauce is said to have originated.
Traditional recipes include minced cornichons, onion, green pepper, and sometimes anchovies.
Many variations exist: some add mustard, Worcestershire sauce, or hot sauce.
It is a staple topping for the classic club sandwich and shrimp cocktail.
In Russia the sauce became popular in the 1990s as a ready‑to‑use salad dressing.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: The mayonnaise base provides vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Plant‑based oils supply monounsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomato ketchup adds lycopene, a compound linked to reduced oxidative stress.

items.title: May provide probiotics (when fermented pickles are used)
items.content: Fermented pickles can contribute beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Low sugar when homemade
items.content: By controlling the amount of ketchup, added sugar can be kept to a minimum.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy base makes the dressing calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sugar and sodium
items.content: Ketchup and pickles add sugar and salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought dressings may contain artificial additives that some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use Thousand Island dressing as a salad dressing, a burger or sandwich sauce, a dip for vegetables or seafood, or stir it into potato salad or egg dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing refrigerated in a sealed container for 2‑3 weeks. Discard if you notice off‑flavors, discoloration, or mold.
